title: The idea of a “multipolar” world
subtitle: After American dominance
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: The world no longer has a single leader. **Multipolarity** is dealing out the cards of power again, and nobody yet knows who will write the new rules.

hero.hook: For twenty years, one country ran the planet. That era is ending.

blocks.text: For a long time, the world was dominated by a single superpower: the United States. The shift toward a world where several centers of power coexist, **multipolarity**, is one of the great turning points of the 21st century.

This change is not only economic. It redefines sovereignty, the strength of alliances and the way conflicts get settled. The end of the Cold War suggested a single unified world order. Reality has turned out to be far messier.

sections.title: From a bipolar balance to American dominance

blocks.text: For almost forty-five years, international relations ran on **bipolarity**: two rival blocs, the West led by the United States through **NATO**, and the East under Soviet influence. That tense balance offered a kind of stability, since neither camp risked a direct clash, thanks to nuclear deterrence.

The fall of the USSR in 1991 ended that standoff. The American columnist **Krauthammer** then spoke of the **[[“Unipolar moment”]]**: for the first time since the Roman Empire, one nation led in every field. The United States became a hyperpower with no credible rival.
The American “unipolar moment,” from 1991 to 2008, was one of the shortest empires in history, ending as China and Russia began to challenge American supremacy.
Those years brought growing intervention: from the Balkans to the Middle East, Washington acted as the “world's policeman,” sometimes with a UN mandate, more and more often alone.

The shift to multipolarity comes from several national paths that all challenge Western dominance. The main engine is the rise of **China**, which became the “factory of the world” before turning its economic weight into military ambition. Through the **[[New Silk Road]]**, Beijing has woven a vast network of influence.

**Russia**, for its part, has staged an aggressive strategic comeback, rejecting the order born in 1991 as humiliating. Other countries, such as **India**, claim strategic autonomy. Many of them meet inside the **[[BRICS]]**, a grouping that lets them push back against the G7.
India shows what this new world looks like: it buys Russian oil despite the sanctions, runs military exercises with the United States, and sits beside China in the BRICS.
Active middle powers such as Turkey complete the picture. The world no longer organizes itself around an ideology, but around a pragmatism in which every player tries to maximize its own sovereignty.
Handling global problems becomes very hard in a multipolar world. The UN Security Council is the clearest example: heavy use of the veto often blocks any effective resolution on major conflicts.

blocks.caption: The rise of several rival powers is redrawing the global balance inherited from the Cold War

blocks.text: Multipolarity also fragments the rules. Where the West defends universal values tied to human rights, the new centers of power often preach non-interference. That makes it harder to fight climate change or to regulate new technologies.

The global economy feels the same tension, through a selective form of deglobalization known as “friend-shoring,” where trade concentrates between countries with matching interests. Far from guaranteeing peace, multipolarity so far seems to produce chronic instability.

sections.title: Risks and opportunities of the new order

blocks.text: For some theorists, such as the American John Mearsheimer, a multipolar world is unstable, because it encourages competition for regional dominance and raises the risk of miscalculation between great powers. With no single protective umbrella left, many countries are rearming.

Yet multipolarity also offers a chance to democratize international relations. For the countries of the Global South, it opens a freedom of choice they never had before: no longer a satellite, but a player able to bargain with several centers of power at once.

The world order is no longer a garden tended by one hand, but a space where several forces live side by side. The stability of the 21st century will rest on everyone's ability to manage clashing interests.
The American “unipolar moment” after 1991 lasted less than twenty years. China, Russia, India and other powers now contest the dominance of any single pole, opening a new era of global competition.
